title: LegionLinearEpochVesting: Non-askToken ERC20 sent to contract is permanently locked
description: LegionLinearEpochVesting.release(address token) is guarded by the onlyAskToken(token) modifier, which reverts for any token other than s_askToken. If any ERC20 token other than askToken is accidentally sent to the vesting contract (e.g., via a mistaken transfer, airdrop, or fee-on-transfer rebate), it cannot be recovered. There is no sweep or emergency withdrawal function on the vesting contract itself. The vestingController can only call emergencyTransferOwnership(), which changes the owner (beneficiary) but does not help recover stuck non-askToken ERC20s. By contrast, LegionLinearVesting.release(token) has no such restriction and allows any token to be released.
vulnerable_code: function release(address token) public override onlyAskToken(token) onlyCliffEnded
contrast: LegionLinearVesting.release(token) has no onlyAskToken restriction — inconsistency between the two vesting contract types
impact: Any non-askToken ERC20 (airdrops, mistaken transfers) sent to an EpochVesting contract is permanently unrecoverable.
recommendation: Add a rescueToken(address token, uint256 amount) function callable by vestingController for non-askToken recovery, or remove the onlyAskToken restriction and instead allow any token release to beneficiary (consistent with LegionLinearVesting).

title: LegionTokenDistributor: referrerFeeReceiver zero address not validated — permanently breaks supplyTokens()
description: LegionTokenDistributor._verifyValidConfig() validates that projectAdmin, addressRegistry, and askToken are non-zero, but does NOT validate that referrerFeeReceiver is non-zero. If a distributor is initialized with referrerFeeReceiver = address(0) and referrerFeeOnTokensSoldBps > 0, then every call to supplyTokens() will attempt safeTransferFrom(askToken, msg.sender, address(0), referrerFee). Standard ERC20 implementations (including OpenZeppelin) revert on transfers to address(0). Since tokensSupplied is a one-time flag that only gets set after the transfer completes, and there is no way to update referrerFeeReceiver after initialization, the contract becomes permanently unable to receive tokens. This makes it impossible for any investor to ever claim their token allocation.
impact: If deployed with referrerFeeReceiver=address(0) and non-zero referrerFee BPS, supplyTokens() permanently reverts and the contract is rendered non-functional. Investors cannot claim any allocated tokens.
note: Requires misconfiguration during initialization. Deployer is a trusted role, but the missing validation is a code-level defect that could be triggered by human error.

title: LegionVestingFactory: Permissionless creation enables fake vesting event pollution and off-chain confusion
description: LegionVestingFactory.createLinearVesting() and createLinearEpochVesting() have no access control (confirmed AC-007 in prior audit, deepening here). Beyond gas waste, any attacker can call createLinearVesting(victimAddress, attackerAddress, ...) which emits NewLinearVestingCreated with victim as beneficiary and attacker as vestingController. Off-chain indexers or monitoring systems that track vesting by beneficiary address will incorrectly associate these fake contracts with real investors. Since the emitted event cannot be distinguished from legitimate protocol-created events, this creates a phishing surface. Furthermore, the attacker-controlled vestingController can call emergencyTransferOwnership() on that fake vesting contract, silently re-assigning the beneficiary role.
impact: Phishing via fake vesting events; off-chain monitoring confusion; investor UX degradation. No direct loss of protocol funds since fake contracts are not registered in TokenDistributor positions.
recommendation: Add onlyOwner or a whitelist of authorized callers (e.g., sale contracts). All other factories in the protocol enforce onlyOwner.
note: This extends finding AC-007 with the event pollution attack vector.

title: LegionLinearEpochVesting & LegionLinearVesting: ETH release() bypasses cliff restriction
description: Both vesting contracts override release(address token) with the onlyCliffEnded modifier to prevent token release before the cliff ends. However, neither contract overrides the ETH release() function inherited from VestingWalletUpgradeable. This means ETH sent to either vesting contract (e.g., via selfdestruct force-send or accidental transfer) can be released to the beneficiary at any time, even before the cliff period ends. This is inconsistent with the cliff enforcement design intent.
impact: ETH accidentally or forcibly sent to vesting contracts can be released before cliff ends. Practical risk is low since the protocol only uses ERC20 tokens.
recommendation: Override the ETH release() function with onlyCliffEnded in both vesting contracts for consistency: function release() public override onlyCliffEnded { super.release(); }

title: LegionVestingManager: Zero-value epoch parameters pass validation, causing permanent DoS via division-by-zero
description: In _verifyValidVestingConfig(), the LEGION_LINEAR_EPOCH validation requires numberOfEpochs * epochDurationSeconds == vestingDurationSeconds. If all three are zero, 0 * 0 = 0 == 0 passes. Combined with cliffDurationSeconds = 0 (which satisfies cliff <= duration), an entirely-zero LegionInvestorVestingConfig for epoch vesting passes all validation checks. When LegionLinearEpochVesting is then deployed with epochDurationSeconds = 0, every call to getCurrentEpoch() executes (timestamp - start) / 0, triggering a Solidity 0.8 PANIC (division by zero). Since getCurrentEpoch() is called from within release() via _vestingSchedule(), all release() calls permanently revert. The investor's vested tokens become irretrievably locked in the contract with no recovery path (no emergencyWithdraw on the vesting contract itself).
impact: If Legion signer issues a vestingSignature for a zero-parameter epoch config (e.g., due to a signing service bug or off-by-one error), the investor's vested tokens become permanently locked. emergencyTransferOwnership only changes the beneficiary, not the epochDuration.
recommendation: Add explicit checks in _verifyValidVestingConfig: require(vestingDurationSeconds > 0) and require(numberOfEpochs > 0 && epochDurationSeconds > 0) for LEGION_LINEAR_EPOCH type.
note: Requires trusted role (Legion signer) to issue a bad signature. However, missing validation is a defense-in-depth gap that could cause irreversible investor loss.

title: LegionReferrerFeeDistributor: Merkle root replacement with lower cumulative amount causes permanent claim DoS via arithmetic underflow
description: claim() computes amountToClaim = amount - s_claimedAmounts[msg.sender], where amount is the value proven by the current Merkle proof. s_claimedAmounts tracks the historical total claimed by each referrer. If Legion replaces the Merkle root with one containing a lower cumulative amount for a referrer who has already claimed (e.g., due to an error or root regeneration), then amount < s_claimedAmounts[msg.sender], causing an arithmetic underflow. Solidity 0.8 converts this to a PANIC revert, permanently blocking that referrer from making any future claims under the new root.
vulnerable_code:
uint256 amountClaimed = s_claimedAmounts[msg.sender];
uint256 amountToClaim = amount - amountClaimed;  // PANIC if amount < amountClaimed
impact: If a new Merkle root is set with a lower cumulative amount than a referrer's already-claimed amount, that referrer is permanently unable to claim future fees from this distributor. emergencyWithdraw by Legion can rescue the tokens, but the referrer loses autonomous claim ability.
recommendation: Add a check before subtraction: if (amount <= amountClaimed) revert (with a clear error). Also add documentation that the Merkle root must always use monotonically increasing cumulative amounts per referrer.
note: setMerkleRoot() is onlyLegion. The underflow requires a Legion error. However, the missing safety check means a Merkle root mistake causes permanent DoS with no graceful degradation.

title: LegionVestingFactory: Event emitted before initialize() completes — violates CEI pattern
description: In both createLinearVesting() and createLinearEpochVesting(), the NewLinearVestingCreated / NewLinearEpochVestingCreated event is emitted BEFORE the initialize() call on the newly cloned contract. While this is not exploitable within the same transaction (no reentrancy vector since initialize is in the same tx), it violates the standard Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern and may mislead off-chain listeners that react to the event before the contract is fully initialized.
impact: Off-chain systems processing events in real-time may interact with an uninitialized clone. Not exploitable on-chain within the same transaction.
recommendation: Move the emit statement to after the initialize() call to follow CEI and to ensure off-chain listeners see a fully initialized contract.

title: LegionLinearEpochVesting: getCurrentEpochAtTimestamp() silently truncates uint256 to uint64
description: getCurrentEpochAtTimestamp(uint256 timestamp) accepts a uint256 input but casts (timestamp - start()) to uint64 before dividing by epochDuration. For very large uint256 inputs (e.g., type(uint256).max), the subtraction result exceeds uint64.max, causing silent truncation to a random uint64 value, which returns a garbled epoch number. This function is public and view-only, so it cannot affect state or release logic (since _vestingSchedule receives a uint64 timestamp from OZ internals). However, off-chain callers or monitoring tools querying this function with arbitrary timestamps may receive incorrect results.
impact: Incorrect epoch returned for large timestamp inputs. View-only; no impact on token release state.
recommendation: Add a bounds check: require(timestamp - start() <= type(uint64).max) or change the return type handling to cap at numberOfEpochs + 1 for values beyond vestingEnd.

title: LegionTokenDistributor: claimAmount not validated on-chain against remaining distribution budget
description: claimTokenAllocation() increments totalAmountClaimed by claimAmount without checking that totalAmountClaimed <= totalAmountToDistribute. The only enforcement is that claimSignature must be issued by legionSigner. If legionSigner issues signatures for a total exceeding totalAmountToDistribute, calls will revert at the SafeTransfer level (insufficient balance) rather than with a clear protocol-level error. This degrades UX and makes accounting opaque.
impact: No direct loss of funds (SafeTransfer reverts protect the contract). Degraded UX if the signing service over-allocates.
